summary: Enhances BGP route refresh with markers for the beginning and end of a refresh, helping fix routing table inconsistencies without disruption. It updates RFC 2918.

plainLanguage.summary: Asking a friend to resend a list is easier if they say start and end. This adds those markers to a BGP refresh.

subtitle: Begin and end markers that let BGP routers check and repair each other's routing tables without disruption.

tldr.problem: Checking for routing inconsistencies between BGP speakers, such as missed route withdrawals, typically meant tedious offline, manual operations. The older route refresh gave no sign of where a refresh started or ended.
tldr.mechanism: The Reserved field of the ROUTE-REFRESH message becomes a Message Subtype. A speaker sends a BoRR message before re-advertising its Adj-RIB-Out and an EoRR message after, so the receiver can mark old routes stale and purge whatever was not refreshed.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2918 and has not been obsoleted. It lets consistency validation happen online and without disruption.

today: RFC 7313 is a Proposed Standard from July 2014 and updates RFC 2918. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Route Refresh Needs Markers
sections.content:
BGP speakers sometimes need to validate routing consistency, for example to catch a missing route withdrawal. The RFC says such checks usually involve offline, manual operations that are tedious and time-consuming.

RFC 2918 already lets a speaker ask a peer to re-advertise its routes. Route refresh, as this RFC uses the term, is the complete re-advertisement of the Adj-RIB-Out to a peer, subject to routing policies. What it lacks is a way to say where that re-advertisement begins and ends. This RFC adds that, so validation can be done online and non-disruptively.
sections.plainLanguage: When a friend resends a long list, you cannot tell when they are done. This RFC makes them say 'start' and 'end' so you know.

sections.title: The New Capability and Message Subtypes
sections.content:
The Enhanced Route Refresh Capability is a new BGP capability, using the mechanism of RFC 5492. IANA assigned it Capability Code 70, and its Capability Length is zero. Advertising it tells a peer that the speaker supports the message subtypes and procedures in this RFC.

The Reserved field of the ROUTE-REFRESH message from RFC 2918 is redefined as the Message Subtype. A speaker that supports the procedures SHOULD advertise the capability, and the procedures apply only once a speaker has received the capability from a peer.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers first tell each other 'I know the start and end trick'. Only then do they use it.

sections.title: Message Subtypes
sections.content:
The redefined field takes these values:

  • 0: a normal route refresh request, with or without Outbound Route Filtering (RFC 5291).
  • 1: BoRR, the demarcation of the beginning of a route refresh.
  • 2: EoRR, the demarcation of the ending of a route refresh.
  • 255: Reserved.

All other values are reserved for future use. A speaker that gets a ROUTE-REFRESH message with a subtype other than 0, 1 or 2 MUST ignore it and SHOULD log an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The message gets a small label: 'please resend', 'I am starting to resend' or 'I am done resending'.

sections.title: How a Refresh Works
sections.content:
Before a speaker starts a route refresh, whether it started locally or answers a normal request from the peer, it MUST send a BoRR message. After it finishes re-advertising the entire Adj-RIB-Out, it MUST send an EoRR message. The 'entire' Adj-RIB-Out means all route entries at the start of the operation, covering both reachability and unreachability information. If an entry changes later, only that entry needs to be advertised.

A BoRR can arrive at any time. On receiving one, the speaker MUST mark all routes from that peer for the given AFI and SAFI pair as stale. Routes that arrive in the re-advertisement replace the matching stale routes. On receiving an EoRR, the speaker MUST immediately remove any routes from that peer still marked stale for that pair, and MAY log them for analysis.

A speaker MAY ignore an EoRR that arrives without a prior BoRR. An implementation MAY also set a locally configurable upper bound on how long stale routes are kept, and remove them without waiting for the EoRR once it is reached.
sections.plainLanguage: When you hear 'start', you put a sticky note on every item you have. Each item that comes again loses its note. At 'end', whatever still has a note gets thrown away.

sections.title: Working with Graceful Restart
sections.content:
The RFC keeps this feature separate from the End-of-RIB (EoR) marker in Graceful Restart (RFC 4724), so that stale routes are not cleaned up too early.

  • A speaker that supports Graceful Restart MUST NOT send a BoRR for an AFI and SAFI before it sends the EoR for that pair to the neighbor.
  • A speaker that has received the Graceful Restart Capability from its neighbor MUST ignore any BoRR for a pair received before it gets the EoR for that pair, and SHOULD log an error.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already an 'I finished my first list' signal for restarts. This rule makes sure the two kinds of 'finished' do not get mixed up.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new NOTIFICATION error code, 7, named ROUTE-REFRESH Message Error, with one subcode: 1, Invalid Message Length. These rules apply only when the speaker has received the Enhanced Route Refresh Capability from the peer.

If the length of a received ROUTE-REFRESH message with subtype 1 or 2 is not 4, excluding the fixed-size message header, the speaker MUST send a NOTIFICATION with that error code and subcode. The Data field MUST contain the complete ROUTE-REFRESH message.
sections.plainLanguage: If a start or end note is the wrong size, the receiver sends back a complaint that includes the bad note.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA assigned Capability Code 70 in the Capability Codes registry. It created a new registry, 'BGP Route Refresh Subcodes', where values 0-127 need Standards Action and values 128-254 are First Come First Served. Values 3-254 are unassigned.

IANA also renamed the 'BGP Error Codes' registry to 'BGP Error (Notification) Codes', allocated the new error code, and created the registry 'BGP ROUTE-REFRESH Message Error subcodes', where 0 is Reserved, 1 is Invalid Message Length and 2-255 are unassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list of numbers was updated so everyone uses the new codes the same way.
